utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, good afternoon in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Today is Thursday, May 22nd, 2008. Let me greet the witness, the Defence counsel, the accused, everyone assisting us in and around the courtroom as well as the Prosecutor. We will now proceed with the testimony and the cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot hear. I cannot hear the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine it's working now. The Prosecutor has two hours and nine minutes left. Let me remind you that today we'll finished at 25 past 6.00. If there aren't any administrative matters to deal with, I'll give the floor to Mr. Scott immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, good afternoon. Good afternoon, counsel, good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the next topic -- and good afternoon, I should say, Dr. Rebic, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you too, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would like to turn from the topic of the law concerning refugees which we ended the day with yesterday to the topic of Croatian citizenship and I heard you testify on Monday that essentially anyone who said "I am Croat," was given Croatian citizenship. I think that's the way you put it; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is correct is that anyone could obtain Croatian citizenship who was able to show the institution granting citizenship, which was the Ministry of the Interior, proof that - and I'm referring to persons from Bosnia and Herzegovina - that they had declared themselves as Croats before and they could prove that by showing a school certificate, for example, because in the former Yugoslavia, ethnicity was recorded on school certificates, or they could use some other document to prove that in which ethnicity was stated. This applied equally to citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina who were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well I'm going to double-check the quotation, and I'll come back to you with that in a moment. I think you were rather direct what you said on Monday about that, but let's turn to Exhibit 1D 02918. Should the -- I believe it's in one of the Defence binders but I may not -- it may be in both actually. It should be in the Prosecution binder if that assists the usher, my apology. It may be in both. Now, there is two aspects of the Statute that I would like to discuss for a few minutes. This is the Law on Croatian Citizenship which was I think first adopted around the -- or effective the 26th of June, 1991. There were amendments in 1992 and 1993 which I understand did not impact or have an effect on the two portions that I am interested in at the moment. If I can ask you, please, to look to Article number 8, Article 8. This appears to be a provision, sir, that would apply -- what I would consider to anyone, anyone anywhere in the world who for whatever reason wanted to obtain Croatian citizenship by a process of naturalization would be able to follow these procedures, apply under this law, and under -- if they satisfied the requirements of Article 8, they had the possibility of obtaining Croatian citizenship; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, I would like to next ask you to look directly at Article 16. If you look at this, there's a specific provision which provides that, it's quite short so I'll just read it, "A member of the Croatian nation who does not have domicile in the Republic of Croatia may obtain Croatian citizenship if he or she meets the conditions from Article 8, paragraph 1, item 5 of this law and if he or she issues a written statement that he or she considers himself or herself to be a Croatian citizen." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, there appear to be then two requirements. One is -- one refers us back to Article 8 which we looked at a moment ago to section 5 or paragraph 5 of Article 8. That requirement says, provides, "That a conclusion can be derived from his or her conduct that he or she respects the legal system and the customs in the Republic of Croatia and that he or she accepts the Croatian culture." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And speaks the Croatian language and the Latin script and so on. There are several clauses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Not under section 5; correct? That's another section.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're right. Yes. So this is about respecting the legal system and customs of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go back to Article 16, or stay on Article 16, it makes reference here and at least the way it's been translated into English, it says, "A member of the Croatian nation." Now, can we understand that to mean a member of the Croatian people? How would you explain the term that's used there? What is a member of the Croatian nation in that context as distinct from citizenship in the Republic of Croatia? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] This is an insult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, Mr. Praljak, you've already taken the floor on umpteenth occasions about this. The Prosecutor is free to say what he wants. You may not agree with him, but on the day you testify, you will be able to develop your own position. No need to start protesting that way. We are perfectly aware of your position. You've already outlined it for us. If the Prosecutor wants to make such a statement, he is perfectly entitled to do so. During the presentation of your case when your witnesses come to testify or when you come to testify, because you've told us that you are going to testify, you will be able to deal with this matter. Please let the Prosecutor put his question and the witness will answer and the answer of the witness may be amenable to you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please, this is not a protest. I simply want to know what is on trial here. Is it talking about the Croatian language? Are we going to deal with Hego [phoen]? How far are we going to go? For ten years, in Switzerland if someone wants to get citizenship, they make sure that he washes the dishes that he does the dishes after dinner and here, someone just has to be a member of the Croatian people. This is an insult on every ground. It's not a protest of mine. What are we talking about? What is this trial about? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may, I do -- I believe the objection is on relevance, and the witness has indicated that the Ministry of the Interior was dealing with this issue. I don't believe that there was testimony on direct examination that he -- that his department was issuing Croatian citizenships to anyone. He hasn't been qualified as an expert on the law. I fail to see now -- there will be, I can assure the Trial Chamber, that there will be in the very, very near future someone who has dealt with this particular law and these questions should be addressed to that person, not -- so I do object on the ground of relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Coric. THE ACCUSED CORIC: [Interpretation] May I please leave the courtroom. I am not feeling as well and I need medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No problem. Please call the Tribunal's physician for Mr. -- and that Mr. Coric should be escorted out of the courtroom immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Mr. Scott, please proceed with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but I do have an objection and I would like a ruling. If this is relevant, I would like to know how is it relevant so I do need -- request a response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to understand your objection, we need to find out what the question is and what the answer of the witness is. You are perfectly right, Mr. Karnavas, the witness is not a lawyer, and he may not be familiar with the law on citizenship in Croatia. There's no doubt about this. However, as a Croatian national, he may have some information about this matter. Let's wait and see what he has to say. If what he has to say is of no relevance, then the probative value will be nil. If it's not the case, then we'll receive. Let's listen to the question and then to the answer of the witness. Mr. Scott, please repeat your question because we've lost track of it after all these exchanges. Please put your question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I do that, and partly to respond to some of the comments that have been made, let me go back and -- now I have found the exact passage from Monday's testimony which indicates that indeed it was raised in direct examination, that this is a witness who works directly in the area of the status of people, refugees, and displaced persons. If he's not qualified to talk about these topics, then it conflicts directly with the responsibilities he's held for some five or six years, but this is what he said on Monday, in any event when asked about, by the Defence: "At that time," at page 28202, "At that time it was enough for a Muslim from Bosnia-Herzegovina to show the department of the ministry of interior any document, a driving licence, a school certificate, which said that he had declared himself to be a Croat at some time ipso facto he had the right to a Croatian certificate of citizenship and Croatian documents." That's what he said and that was not -- that was in response to Defence questioning on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm now showing you a document which is itself a Defence Exhibit 1D 02918. And there was nothing intended to be offensive about my question to you. When we look at Article 16 the way it's been translated to me is that it says, "A member of the Croatian nation." Now, I've also seen another translation of the name provision which says, "A member of the Croatian people." Now, all I'm saying here is we're talking here about something that's different than Croatian citizenship. Obviously if one had Croatian citizenship -- being a member of the Croatian nation is having citizenship, there's no reason for the Statute. If you had citizenship you wouldn't be applying for it. So it says, "A member of the Croatian nation who does not have domicile in the Republic of Croatia may obtain Croatian citizenship ..." these two requirements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Mr. Coric's counsel wants to take the floor. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may be given a break of two or three minutes, the guards are calling me to come outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was about to suggest that you go see your client. Please do. Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Picking up from what we've covered, sir. When I read those two provisions in this context concerning a person who does not have a domicile in the Republic of Croatia, it strikes me that establishing that you respect the legal system and customs in the Republic of Croatia and that you accept Croatian culture for someone who doesn't live there and saying that you consider yourself to be Croatian is essentially one and the same thing, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Mr. Coric's counsel will give us some news about her client. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may we move into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Dr. Rebic, a lot has happened in the last 45 minutes or so so let me go back to -- if you still have Exhibit 1D 02918, The Law on Croatian Citizenship in front of you, Article -- and again looking primarily at Article 16. And I believe my pending question to you was something and it's no longer of course on the screen at this point, but my question was something to the following effect and that is: Since Article 16 specifically addresses the situation, we're talking about someone who does not have a domicile, does not live in Croatia, but would apply, obtain -- would like to obtain Croatian citizenship, how would such a person demonstrate that he or she respects the legal system and customs in the Republic of Croatia and that he or she accepts the Croatian culture other than a written statement, I suppose, certification to that effect?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, first of all, I'm quite taken aback to find myself in a position to offer legal interpretation of Croatian legislation. Secondly, the Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons held no competencies in terms of giving or taking away the citizenship from anyone, we simply did not deal with such matters. However, as a layperson, I may still offer a clarification concerning a statement I gave to the Defence. In order to understand that, one needs to know that in the Croatian language, there are two expressions, one is drzavljnstvo, citizenship, the other one is narodnost, ethnicity. The Croatian citizenship be can be received by both members of the Croatian people, the Serbian people, or any of the other minorities, these being Czechs, Slovaks, Italians, Hungarians, et cetera. As regards the Muslims, one also needs to know that many Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina declared themselves as Croats. It had been like that for decades. That is why those Muslims who felt themselves to be members of the Croatian people living outside the borders of the Republic of Croatia, of course in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well as in other countries of the world, those people who felt themselves to be Croatian, not as of yesterday or dating back to their father but generations back, those people who declared themselves to be Croatian and believed to be part of the Croatian culture, when such a person had to flee to Croatia, which by that time had become an independent state, giving Croatian citizenship although it had existed in some shape or form in the former Yugoslavia, that person was entitled to a Croatian citizenship by virtue of not only an oral statement but also by a piece of paper, a document. That could have been a certificate, a school certificate, a military booklet in which I also stated I was Croatian alongside my colleague, Ibro Ibrisimovic, who also declared himself to be Croatian. I am not speaking as a lawyer, I am speaking as someone who is rather familiar with history, with the situation in my homeland. So I ask you, how do you deny that person the feelings they have and something they've always stated all along.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me be very clear about this, and there was no reason for anyone to outburst or for anyone to take offence before. It was a question which you've now attempted to answer and I have a couple follow-up questions, but no one is intending to insult you or anyone's Croatness so please, we should take that as a further starting point. The point is, sir, how is someone -- no. Listen to my question.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, Mr. Scott. No offence taken. No offence taken. However, I wanted to add another thing. Being Croatian does not include faith or religion. A Croatian could be Catholic, Orthodox, Muslim, Protestant, et cetera. One should never think that there is a sign of equation between Croatian and Catholic. It includes Croats, Muslims, and other ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me go back to the question now that you've given us that further explanation. Thank you. Let me go back to my specific question. You have a person, and I'll use your example, of a Muslim, who is in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He has never lived in Croatia before, ever before. How would that person demonstrate that he respects, he or she, would establish -- to meet the requirement that he or she respects the legal system and customs in the Republic of Croatia and that he or she accepts the Croatian culture? You can't say, "I've lived in Croatia for 20 years. Of course I've always obeyed the law, I've never even received a traffic ticket. I belong to the Croatian culture club. I go to all the dinners." I'm not being facetious, but if you lived in Croatia, what I'm giving you is a scenario. Someone who lives in Bosnia, someone who lives in Australia, they've never lived in Croatia before so how is that -- but they consider themselves Croats. So how is that person going to establish that he or she respects the legal system and customs in the Republic of Croatia and accepts Croatian culture?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It fell inside the remit of those people who lived in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs its department in charge of issuing the document, which is called domovnica, which is a certificate of citizenship as well as to issue passports. Some people in Bosnia-Herzegovina accepted Croatian -- the Croatian culture. Part of the Croatian literature was created by Muslims. One needs to have some historical knowledge to be able to address that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification for the record, on page 13, line 16, the gentleman indicated "those who worked" as opposed to "lived" in the ministry of foreign affairs. It's kind of difficult to live in the ministry of foreign affairs, so it's those who worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let's go forward. I think perhaps the citizenship will come up, issues will come up in other context.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Related to what we've been talking about in the last few minutes, in fact, is the next question, that is, that there is evidence that President Tudjman espoused the view that Bosnian Muslims were Croats of Islamic faith and is that or has that ever been your view?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my view, based on my lifetime experience and my experience from the youth and the army that there were Muslims of Croatian nationality -- well, those who belonged to the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I'm not -- sir, my question is not whether there were individual Muslims who considered themselves Croats but that the people, to the extent there were people that considered themselves might otherwise call themselves now Bosniaks or Bosnian Muslims, but President Tudjman espoused the view that Muslims, these Bosnian Muslims were Croats, they were Croats who had taken on the Islamic faith. Now, is that your view or have you ever held that view?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One cannot opine on that. These are facts. One either accepts them or denies them. However, you cannot have an opinion on facts. It is a fact that at a certain point in history, a large part of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina was the territory of the Croatian state until the Turks invaded parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the 15th century. Throughout the 16th, 17th and 18th century, the Turks imposed Islam upon the Croatian people who lived in what is today Bosnia-Herzegovina. The same way they imposed Islam on the Serb people, those who were of orthodox faith. It is a fact and not a matter of my opinion, a part of the Croatian people who lived in Bosnia-Herzegovina was forced to take on Islam. It is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going back to the refugee situation in Croatia, is it correct that the -- at some point, perhaps in 1992, 1993, perhaps you can tell us if you know, that the Croatian government in terms of Muslims coming to Croatia from Bosnia or elsewhere, I suppose, but in terms of these Muslim persons that were fleeing or moving out of Bosnia, that they were primarily moved to four collective officers, that being Gasinci, Obonjan, Varazdin and Samobor. In fact I believe that was during the late summer and autumn of 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say predominantly in those centres, that is correct. But however these were not the only centres. There were many more refugee centres which accommodated refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina who were of Muslim faith. In Zagreb alone, there were several --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who made the decision, sir, to make those essentially the four principal centres, was that your decision as head of ODPR or if it wasn't your decision, whose decision was it?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was nobody's decision. There were no main or principal centres. There were around four -- 500 centres housing refugees and displaced persons. There were no principal centres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please -- there is something that is very important for me, so I'm just coming back to what you said earlier concerning the assessment of the issue raised in the indictment. You said that the Turks had invaded Bosnia-Herzegovina in the 17th and 18th century and they forced Croatians to become Muslims and these Croatians became Muslims at the time. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do have a correction to make. The Turks began occupying Bosnia-Herzegovina as early as the late 15th century and then throughout the 16th and 17th century. Occasionally, they imposed Islam on the Catholics there, not upon the Croats there, because they can be forced to take on Islam however they remain Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 15th century there were Croatians who with time ended up becoming Muslims. They became Muslims. And in 1991, 1992, 1993, some, some of them -- or some people, sorry, believed that Muslims in Bosnia are Croatians because they belong to this Croatian nation which may either be in Croatia, Australia, the United States or anywhere in the world. Is that what you told us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In principle, that is so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which means that when Muslims from Bosnia-Herzegovina -- let's take people for instance coming from Mostar, when they come -- go to Croatia, you could then consider them as Croatians and based on their identity papers or based on school certificate or whatever paper, you could give them Croatian citizenship. When I say "you" I mean Croatia, the Ministry of the Interior. That we got.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, when there were Muslims from Mostar arriving in the Republic of Croatia, they were largely without any papers and documents. Those of them who wanted to receive the Croatian citizenship, that is those who felt to be Croatian, how they went about that, I don't know. That depended upon them alone. As for Mostar, I wanted to say that between the two world wars, the Muslims in Mostar predominantly declared themselves to be Croats. After World War II, the situation was quite different through the pressure exercised by the Serbian politics which no longer allowed those Muslims to declare themselves to be Croats. That is why a new term was introduced, non-affiliated. Many Muslims accepted that, however my friend whom I mentioned a few moments ago, Ibro Ibrisimovic did not accept that and stated that he was Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to go one step further than this. For, let's say, hundreds of years, the Turks were there, now did the Turks in some way mix with the domestic population, were there intermarriages and is there any record on whether those who live there now descend entirely or partly from Turkish parents, I suppose mainly the fathers. Can you tell us something about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you put a question to me which would take a few hours for me to answer; however, since I need to be brief I can tell you this: When the Croatian --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's Croatian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- when the Turkish army arrived in certain parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina since we were occupying Bosnia-Herzegovina through decades part by part then of course there were mixed marriages, that is to say that certain Turkish soldiers married Christian women and they took Croatian children. Thousands upon thousands of children were taken away by force from their parents and taken back to Turkey in order to make them orthodox Muslims. Some of them, through individual contacts and throughout history, declared themselves to be of Croatian descent. There is an anecdote Padre Drkolica [phoen] who was a Franciscan monk in Jerusalem in the 16th century received from the Jerusalem vizier to build a tower next to the basilica of Jesus Christ and to renew it thanks to his friendship with the vizier. As history states, they drank coffee together and spoke Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if we can touch on some additional information about the refugee situation in Croatia, I would ask -- like you to turn to, if you can find 1D 02626. This is an ODPR report dated the 12th of June, 1998. And if I can direct your attention, please, to part 3, Roman numeral III of the report which is entitled, "Refugees from BiH and Republic of Croatia data per year." Then below that, there is a number one and in that first paragraph, the last sentence says, "Until the end of 1992 in Croatia, large groups of refugees were arriving and it was impossible to give refugee status to new comers and register them." Now, this takes us back to the topic that we were discussing yesterday in connection with the decision of 13th of July 1992, this statement appears to indicate that -- through the balance of that year, 1992, people arriving in Croatia were not given refugee status, legal refugee status; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, that is incorrect. You said that the decision was from July, I believe you said the 13th of July, 1992, however, I believe it was on the 13th of July 1993 if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You are mistaken, sir. We covered this extensively yesterday and I showed you documentation, July, 13th of July 1992, and this says that until the end of 1992, and it was impossible to give refugee status to new comers and register them. So after July, am I correct sir, taking what we discussed yesterday, and taking this report, which is a report from your agency, that people who arrived after the 13th of July, 1992, they may have arrived, they may have been assisted by someone but they were not given legal refugee status; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then if we can go to 1D 02628, we'll come back to that document momentarily if people want to keep their hand on it or close by. If we can go momentarily to 1D 02628 in the Defence binders. Again this document was shown to you during the Defence questioning and the same page. If I can ask you to find again, and I'm using the page numbers if you'll notice on the bottom right corner of the page, there is a 8 digit number with a hyphen in between 1D 34-something if you will find the page where that is 0596. 0596, that is the page I would like you to look at, please.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have 0576 and you're asking for 0596. I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we looked at this briefly yesterday and it appears -- if we look at the period from approximately March 1993 when -- I'm looking at the refugee column, it says there were -- excuse me a moment -- excuse me, April 1993 --

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] April, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In April, we have 269.000, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you turn to the next page, July 1994, July 1994, we have 266.000, approximately.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1994, in April, there are 272.000. That is more than in April the year before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Listen to my question. We seem to be having difficulty communicating today, sir. If you would listen to my questions, please, and answer my questions. I didn't ask you about April. I asked you about July 1994, do you understand?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, Dr. Rebic. Do you understand July 1994?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 266.056, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, I see. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So it appears, sir, that from that -- during that -- 14, 15-month period, there was actually quite a period of stability, the range in there is I think something less than 10 per cent of a variation where with a small peak in, I believe February of 1994, 284 -- approximately 284.000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. The influx changed up and down depending on the old ones leaving and new ones arriving. Some people were returning to Bosnia-Herzegovina, some were departing for third countries. That is why you see such slight differences which are quite understandable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if we go back to the other document, 1D 02626, the one that we were looking at before. If you're still on -- again in section number III or part III -- perhaps the usher can assist me?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Excuse me, Mr. Scott. I don't find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. We will assist you, sir.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Scott. It wasn't in the binder. It was on the desk next to the binder. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Not a problem. There is a lot of paper for everyone to look at. If you can go back to part III, section numbered one that we were looking at a moment ago and go to the next paragraph, it says, "In May 1993, after the re-registration of refugees, 271.096 refugees from BiH got refugee status." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, yes, I do. That was in May 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if we go then down, then, if I can just -- in order to find out how many of those approximately were Muslim, if you go to section number 2, the numbered part 2 on the left side, also in reference to May 1993, in that sentence, it tells us that of that 271.000, approximately, 157.000 or almost -- approximately 58 per cent were Muslim. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I don't see but I remember that [Interpretation] Yes, I remember that. This is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And were these Muslims that had been given refugee status by the state of Croatia, legal refugee status as of the 13th of July, 1992, or when had these Muslims been given refugee status?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both before and after. As I said yesterday the ODPR, regardless of the law, I won't say illegally, but regardless of the law granted refugee status to many people because there was simply nothing else to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So what -- do I understand, then, that the decision, the government decision of the 13th of July, 1992 remained in effect, that additional new refugee status not be given but you're saying that your agency went ahead and did it anyway?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were instances where it did, but in any case, it took care of refugees, even if they weren't formally granted refugee status. As we saw yesterday from Mr. Mazowiecki's report, in Varazdin there were refugees, Bosniak Muslims from Bosnia-Herzegovina who were not registered, and I observed at the time that in spite of this, they had been provided with accommodation, protection, and everything else in spite of the fact that they had no document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if we go to part number III, still in the same part number III, again section number 2, the next paragraph starts off by saying, a reference to a decrease. It says, "The most significant reason for decreased number of refugees in Croatia in May 1993 compared to the situation in 1992 was departure of a large number of refugees to third countries." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was certainly -- there was certainly many instances of departure to third countries because in Croatia, the resources had been exhausted and the UNHCR and some other countries offered to take in refugees, or rather, the UNHCR offered to help and some countries regardless of the UNHCR offer to take in refugees and this alleviated the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I can ask you to look at footnote 3 in the document, if you go down a page or two or wherever it might be in the Croatian language document but if you can find footnote 3 and for the English it's on the bottom of page 4.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It says, "The best example of the large number of transits through Croatia was the refugee settlement Gasinci near Djakovo through which more than 25.000 refugees, mostly Muslims, passed within four years of its existing." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For the record, footnote 3 relates to as early as mid-1995 so let's be fair to the witness. He's talking 1992, 1993. Now this is in relation to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Gasinci was one of the four primary refugee collection centres together with Obonjan, Samobor, and Varazdin?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again I object because the gentleman indicated that it wasn't primary. He indicated that there were some 500 refugee centres that had Muslims as well as Croats and that there was no such thing as a primary centre. So I object to this nature of the question because it's been asked, it's been answered, and the gentleman was corrected and I think this is now being unfair to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think the word -- if we're going to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it's argumentative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we're going to parse words, Mr. Karnavas, that he said that those were the four predominant centres, and the word is "predominant," and that is in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if we can look then next, sir, in the third or fourth paragraph --

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me. I didn't say they were predominant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We'll go back in the transcript, sir. Just a moment. If this is what we're going to have to do then I guess it's what we'll have to do.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance while you are looking, what I said was that they were the largest centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. They were the four largest centres?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could direct your attention in the same section 2 of the document, if we go down it's not entirely clear the way the breaks are whether it's the third -- continuation of the third paragraph or the fourth paragraph, but in reference again when it talks about the persons going to third countries, there is a paragraph above that says, "42.076 refugees, mostly Muslims, left Croatia for third countries. Western European and trans oceanic, et cetera." Section 2, it's the third paragraph under the section 2, it's Article 3 -- whatever, it does become confusing, Article 3, Roman numeral III, number 2 on the left side of the page, below that, approximately the third paragraph is a paragraph that begins with the numbers 42.076; do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Mostly Muslims. This means that there were Croats among them too. Yes, I'm aware of that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then in that same paragraph it goes on to say, "There were only few Croats in that figure due to the criteria that were set within relocation programme. Namely, BiH Croats had the right to dual citizenship and among the recipient countries, there was a common position that BiH Croats had the second home country that could take care of them." That is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So the persons, the refugees in Croatia that were primarily going out to third countries were Muslims, according to this report. There were only few Croats among them; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, because third countries did not wish to take in persons who had Croatian citizenship, so persons with Croatian citizenship remained in our refugee centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, if we go to part number -- Roman numeral III, a moment please, we'll still in Roman numeral III, my apology, and if you go to section numbered 12, there's various -- the document goes on and if you get on to the part, please, that is paragraph number 12. About two-thirds of the way through that paragraph it says, "A larger -- a large number of refugees who no longer have the status (due to their own decision or revoked status) have stayed in Croatia on the basis of Croatian citizenship, at least 140.000 of them." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is -- excuse me, we can all read this but this is 1998 that we're referring to. I fail to see the relevancy of all of this because somebody who is enjoying quite a comfortable living standard, who is getting an education there, might decide to stay there but I don't see the relevancy to the indictment. I really don't. Is the Croatian government on trial here? What is this case about now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I find it difficult to see what you're trying to establish. I may understand at the end, you never know, but the Defence is telling us that you are referring to something that happened in 1998. You should not mix apples and pears. What's happened in 1998 is not relevant for 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's our position that this is statistical information going back and covering a wide period of time including back into 1993, 1992, and the point is, and that's the reason for the questions about Croatian citizenship, that there was a substantial difference in the treatment between persons who came from Bosnia who had Croatian citizenship and those which did not. And that's our position and that's what the documents we submit show.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, but why is that relevant? But why is it relevant to the indictment? Every country can make a decision as to who they are going to invite and who are they going to extend citizenship to. If you go to the United States, for instance, it's very difficult to get citizenship. I don't see what the problem is in how it's connected to the joint criminal enterprise. I'm not trying to disrupt the proceedings but I don't -- I think we're far afield at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, your objection has been recorded on the transcript. Let's hear Mr. Scott. Mr. Scott, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I mediate here. This really refers to 1995. It says compared to the situation in 1995. In 1995, mass return did begin, return of Muslims to Bosnia-Herzegovina, on a large scale because in the second half of 1995, after Operation Storm and the liberation of parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well as occupied parts of Croatia, the situation as regards security changed dramatically and that's why a lot of Muslims decided to go back to Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we go back to the third paragraph of part III, back on the page we were looking at before, it tells us, sir, toward the end of that paragraph, it's in 1990 --

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number three, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Roman numeral III, the section paragraphed number 1, the third paragraph in that section. Sorry that's the way the document has been organised. In that paragraph it says, "Until the end of 1993," you'll see around 20.000 -- it says, "around 20.000 refugees arrived in the first inflow during the summer and autumn 1993, and additional 15.000 at the end of 1993 and the beginning of 1994. At first they stayed in the territory of BiH under the HVO control. A smaller number of refugees from those territories stayed in Croatia in 1993." Now does that appear to you to be consistent that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this says -- I'm talking about -- if you go back up, "Around 20.000 refugees arrived in the first inflow during the summer and autumn of 1993," do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. But we had already reached the end of the paragraph where it says in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps if you will listen to my questions, we can proceed more efficiently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I'm sorry, this is not justified. You said 1993 and on the paper, it says 1992 and the witness correctly stated this and there's nothing that was -- you simply misspoke and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, the sentence says, "Around 20.000 refugees arrived in the first inflow during the summer and autumn 1993."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And what's the last figure? Yes, you were going down to the end of the paragraph and what's the last figure there?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It was 1992, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: But you said 1993 there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I misspoke, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, that's okay. It's no crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, does that appear to you to be the -- an accurate statement as you recall it of the inflow of refugees to Croatia from Bosnia-Herzegovina during that time period? The first inflow being about 20.000 in summer and autumn 1993 and an additional 15.000, that is a total of 35.000, at the end of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that that's how it was. Whether the numbers are absolutely precise, I can't say, but in general, yes, I agree with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, out of the 20.000 refugees who arrived in the summer and autumn 1993, and plus the 15.000 -- 15.000 that arrived at the end of 1993, a total of 35.000 refugees, were they mixed, both Croats and Muslim? In the last paragraph, reference is made to the month of July, 22nd of July, 33.000 refugees returned from Bosnia who remained in Croatia and out of these 33.000 refugees, or amongst them, there were 30.000 Croats and 3.000 Muslims. Do you agree with the figures we see here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see the figure of 33.000. Now, after a lapse of 15 years, I can't tell you whether this is absolutely precise. I would have to check all the documents in the binders in our office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but if we read this last sentence, we get the impression that those who arrived after the 13th of July -- after July 1994, there are only -- there are 33.000 in total, 30.000 Croats and 3.000 Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct because at that time, there was a conflict between the Muslims and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina and there were very many victims among the Croats because Croats who were expelled from the enclaves that the Muslims took over. The Muslims expelled those Croats and in the end, they ended up in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any case, what this document seems to be telling us is that in 1993, there were 35.000 new refugees, new refugees, but out of this total, we do not have a distribution for 1993 between Muslims and Croats. We have that distribution for 1994 but not for 1993. Please proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we could go forward, please, sir to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can go forward, sir, I understand that in May of 1993, you had -- you went on a mission to Bosnia-Herzegovina I think with Dr. Granic. This was something that was I think sometimes referred to as the Turkish-Croatian good will mission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say Turkish-Croatian, I would simply call it a good will mission. The members of that good will mission were representatives of the Republic of Croatia, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Turkey.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you went with Dr. Granic as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you go into east Mostar on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did go to east Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what can you tell the Judges about the conditions that you found there in the latter part of May 1993?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the latter part of May 1993, there was still a conflict between the two sides. When we crossed over from western to eastern Mostar, we were under fire coming from the Muslim side. We were receiving signals that it was very dangerous, that we should bend down and so on. When we arrived in eastern Mostar, we were received by General Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps you could answer my question in terms of what conditions did you find in east Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can speak about is the impression I had because I didn't spend a long time in eastern Mostar, only a few hours. My impression was that it was chaos among the people, and I barely managed to save my own life.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was there -- had there been resistance on the part of the delegation, on the Croatian members of the delegation to go into east Mostar at all, that they would -- there was a desire not to go into east Mostar but only to say on the western side?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Scott, on the contrary. All of us, those from Croatia, Turkey, and Bosnia-Herzegovina, we all wanted to go to east Mostar. Moreover, we were supposed to go as far as Tuzla and we wanted to do that, but we were not allowed to by General Pasalic. He wouldn't allow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I understand from the information that we've been provided that you did not meet -- we talked with Dr. Prlic yesterday and you did not have any dealings or you did not meet Dr. Prlic during this trip to Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having met Mr. Prlic on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, directing your attention further into 1993, and around the middle of July 1993, did you become aware of discussions about opening --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Very brief question. You went to Mostar with a delegation and you wanted to go to east Mostar but General Pasalic did not agree. If I understand correctly, there were Turks in the delegation. Didn't they protest because it was quite natural for them to go and see the Muslims? What about the Turks who were with you, didn't they say anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, they did. They did protest. They certainly wanted to go on together with us, the rest of us, but General Pasalic, the leader of the Muslim part in eastern Mostar did not allow it. He said to us, "From this point on, I will not provide you with security escorts on the road." And what else could we do without security escorts but go back? I remember that at that meeting with General Pasalic, there was a lively discussion and that he was very arrogant that he attacked the Croats and wouldn't let them get a word in edgeways. To such an extent that the lady minister from the Turkish delegation said to us, "I'm surprised. We were received better by the Croats in west Mostar than by the Muslims here."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time the Spanish battalion of UNPROFOR was there, couldn't you have asked them to take you there in their armoured vehicles, to take you to Mostar east that way? Didn't you have that idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my recollection, UNPROFOR did assist us but very little and they, themselves, seemed to be afraid. The Spanish battalion, which was supposed to come and collect us after the meeting with General Pasalic, came to pick up our delegation in haste and I was among the last to leave because I couldn't find my driver, so I jumped on to an UNPROFOR vehicle, and that's how I managed to get out alive and I left my coat behind. That's the story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Dr. Rebic, I think there's been a bit of confusion caused. My understanding is, and correct me if I am wrong, I think the confusion is on my part. You and your delegation did go into east Mostar and had a tour there for, I think you earlier said, several hours, but you were not able to go on to Tuzla or Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, going forward to July of 1993, and your position is as head of the Croatian ODPR, did you become aware of any discussions to open what was called a transit centre at the Ljubuski detention facility in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, which centre do you have in mind exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There was a place in Ljubuski, a place called Ljubuski, I don't know if you've ever been there or not, perhaps, where there was a place where Muslim people were being held, detained?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. Did it come to your attention around that time of a proposal put forward by the HVO to operate a transit centre at the Ljubuski detention camp?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I am not familiar with that. I know of something else that you will probably get to later. As for Ljubuski, I don't know anything, at least I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, lest we be diverted by some sort of -- just again, a confusion in language or translation, what is it -- tell me what it is you're familiar with and perhaps we can see if we're talking about the same thing or not.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was wondering, Mr. Scott, whether we were on the same page. May I be of assistance?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it, perhaps, the town of Caplina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No. That's not what we're talking about, I'm sorry. Thank you sir for your trying to help. We'll --

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we could go, Your Honour, into private session, I have a document -- exhibit to show to the witness that is under seal and also not to be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, sir, to turn to Exhibit P 10412. P 10412 which should be in one of the Prosecution binders. Sir, this appears to be a Reuters news article dated the 22nd of July 1993, and in the first paragraph, it says, "Croatia will not accept any more Muslim refugees from Bosnia without UN consent in order to avoid accusations of being implicated in ethnic cleansing, a Croatian official said on Thursday. "Croatia will stop accepting Muslim refugees from Bosnia without previous accord with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees so that it would not be interpreted in the west as ethnic cleansing, Adalbert Rebic head of the government's office for refugees told a news conference." Is that an accurate report on what was said -- what you said on the 22nd of July, 1993 as best you recall?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be true partially, although based on a news report, I cannot prove or deny anything. The media frequently acted unprofessionally, superficially and in a hostile way when it comes to Croatia, especially when Reuters is concerned. However, it was one of the reasons due to which we said that we would have to stop receiving Bosnian-Herzegovinian refugees because there was an increase of accusations in the media that we were helping the Serbs to ethnically cleanse Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, what else could we do but to say, "Very well, then, we will no longer be taking in refugees," because our receiving them and accommodating them was being misinterpreted by some media as well as in certain diplomatic circles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The article says that -- toward the bottom, it says, "Until a few weeks ago, the foreign press was accusing Croatia of closing its borders for refugees, but as soon as we take them in they accuse us of ethnic cleansing." Now, sir, this is yet again, as we've been discussing since yesterday, another reference to the fact that Croatia's borders up until sometime previous to this article had been closed to refugees. So can you tell us again if they had been closed, when -- is this the first instance when they had been opened again in connection with sending these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is an abuse of the process. This question, the way it's phrased is improper. Look -- this is a Reuters and of course we don't have a particular time, they're saying and it's a quote, "Until a few weeks ago, the foreign press was accusing Croatia," in other words, and now, we see no matter what Croatia does, it finds itself in a bind. That's why if the gentleman was allowed to finish his previous answer, which was, "This is why we want the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees to be involved so there would be no accusations of ethnic cleansing on the part of Croatia for accepting refugees." So we have to be fair to the gentleman. And if you look at the quote, the quote speaks for itself. But to misuse the words of the quote, to fit it into some kind of a nepherious and sinister manner, I object to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the quotation is attributed to you on the 22nd of July 1993, "Until a few weeks ago," I take it that means until a few weeks prior to 22 July 1993, "Until a few weeks ago, the foreign press was accusing Croatia of closing its borders." Now, what can you tell us about the complaints or the accusations that around that time, until a few weeks ago, Croatia was being accused of Croatia closing its borders, so what was the foreign press saying a few weeks before the 22nd of July 1993?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading the Croatian text. Well, the Serbian text, in this case. "Until a week ago, the foreign press was accusing Croatia for closing down its border for refugees but now that we are receiving them, we are being accused of ethnic cleansing." That is precisely so. We were in dire straits at the time. If we tried going one way, we were accused of this. If we tried the other way, we were accused of that. Often, it was difficult for one to decide, except to follow one's conscience. We decided that we would take in those who reached Croatia and as far as I can remember, the border was never closed for refugees of any ethnicity. And to repeat, I don't trust Reuters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you're an expert in media because you have had a lot of interviews with the media and I'm not going to enter into more details, but you know as well as I do that when a journalist quotes with inverted come a statement made by a third party, the quotation are almost 100 per cent reliable otherwise this would be a very serious breech of the code of the ethics, and particularly as when it comes to such a famous agency as Reuters it cannot allow itself to quote -- to misquote people because this would go against the reputation of its agencies. It would undermine the reputation of the agency. You say that they made a mistake. Maybe, but some of your statements have been quoted between inverted commas and normally when a journalist gives quotations, normally these quotations are what he heard from the people -- the person he was interviewing. That's a general rule which applies to journalism.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, indeed I have a lot of experience with the media. Until this day, in Croatia, and with foreign media, my experience still is that they do not convey my statement precisely or if they quote it precisely, they put it in the wrong context. To go back to this text, what I said here is true. I am not disputing these statements. Previously, I said that in principle, I do not trust Reuters and that based on their reports, I wouldn't dare try and prove anything since they had a certain position towards Croatia. It stemmed out of a certain policy direction that was applied to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Fair enough. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask you to next go to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask you next to go to a document which I believe we've seen before, P 10048. It's in the Defence binders. Sir, we've looked at -- I believe we've all looked at this document perhaps more than once since you've been here. What -- it was specifically in connection with moving prisoners or people from I think about a thousand Muslims from the Mostar area to Gasinci, and do you recall that being the particular circumstances in which you issued this document which on the subject line says, "Approval for entry and temporary stay in Republic of Croatia"?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, the document was not signed by me. What the document is trying to say is something that becomes clearer if one goes to similar documents which were issued by the ODPR upon request by the UNHCR whenever there was a request to accept refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to provide them with a temporary accommodation in Gasinci or at any other refugee centre. It mostly dealt with Gasinci because the UNHCR had its office there. In 1993, due to the impossibility of Croatia taking in any more refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina, this came about as a consequence. The UNHCR more frequently took part in the resolving of the problem of refugees to the extent possible they took them to third countries, those who could not be taken away stayed with us in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did your agency, sir, play any role in the collection or verification of what was called the letters of guarantee? That was supposed to be part of the package, if you will, for these people to be able to leave where they were in Bosnia and in theory transit through Croatia to a third country?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, there were different and many cases. There were cases in which the UNHCR would compile a list of those they want to send to third countries who were supposed to transit through Croatia. They would then ask for temporary accommodation. There were also instances in which refugees arrived without a list. The regional centre or the social welfare centre that was competent was supposed to register them. All that documentation is kept in the archives of the ODPR until the present day. The third set of circumstances involved --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question, sir, was if you could describe any role that your agency played, if any, in the collection or verification of the document which has called in this courtroom, "the letter of guarantee." Did your agency, the ODPR of Croatia, have anything to do with the preparation of those guarantees, obtaining the guarantees, verifying? What role, if any, did your agency have in connection with those guarantees?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, yes and no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Depending on what?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall what the situation was concerning the 500 people coming in connection with your letter or your agency's letter of 16 July 1993? Do you know whether these people had letters of guarantee at all?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I cannot know that since I did not sign the document. Probably that day, on that occasion, or that week, I was not in Zagreb. Actually, I remember, I was in Geneva at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to next go to, please, Exhibit P 03708. It's in the Defence binder, my apology. Do you have it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. This, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This appears to be a letter that you wrote or at least someone wrote, perhaps you can tell us if that's your signature on the -- at the end of the letter, is that your signature or did someone else sign it for you or what can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, the signature is mine. It is authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You indicated at one point, and I think in the English translation, at least it's at the bottom of the second page, and again you make this point that was referenced in the news article that we looked at earlier, at one point it says, "... we will receive Muslim refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina only in agreement with UNHCR for the purpose of bringing them together with their family members in third countries." Was that, in fact the -- is it your position that that was, in fact, the position of your agency and that policy was implemented from the middle of July 1993 onward? That your agency was not involved in moving any transport, transit, what have you, the movement of any Muslims out of Bosnia and Herzegovina that did not have UNHCR approval?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who did not have UNHCR approval, that is to say that the UNHCR had promised to have them moved on to third countries, were received by the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you're saying they then stayed in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. If we are referring to the same text on page 2, I'll read it in English, if I may, [In English] "the current policy," [Interpretation] is that the text you're referring to? [In English] "In accordance with the current policy."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe so. Yes. The statement goes on further on that page?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. In accordance with the policy so far, we have drawn no distinctions between Muslims and Croats as you are doing. In hotels, we have both Muslims and Croats just as we have Croats in refugee centres as well. Proof of this is Spansko where -- there are both Muslims and Croats in Spansko; that is, and then there is another one where there are Croats from Vukovar. You do have the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, I referred it to you a few minutes ago. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For the purpose of the context I would ask that the entire paragraph, following paragraph, be taken into consideration with Mr. Scott's previous question with reference to UNHCR because it's quite clear why Dr. Rebic is making sure that UNHCR should be involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question was never about what the letter says but whether, in fact, that was the policy of ODPR and whether that policy was followed consistently after July -- middle of July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So is it your position, Dr. Rebic, that this -- these Judges should understand that any of these scenarios after July 1993 occurred only with UNHCR approval? Is that what you're telling this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott, but Mr. Karnavas is right. The passage which follows is very important for an understanding of the situation. I will read it out --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please, please, answer my question, sir. Dr. Rebic, listen to my question. My question is not -- we have the document -- letter in front of us we've all read it. Everyone in the courtroom has read it, do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question to you was: Was that, in fact, obeyed, the position of -- there will be no more sending whatever word, I'm trying to think of a neutral word so I don't get an objection, we will not transit any more Muslims through Croatia, they will not take any more Muslims from Bosnia-Herzegovina unless we have UNHCR approval. Was that your position and was that, in fact, carried out from July 1993 forward?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We need to take the 20-minute break. You will have 50 minutes left, Mr. Scott. I hope there won't be too many objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Five zero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Five zero. 50. Five zero.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't think so. But okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask the registrar to check again. He told me a few minutes ago that Mr. Scott has used -- had used three hours and 22 minutes. Mr. Scott had four hours and 15 minutes because you yourself used 15 additional minutes, so in other words, Mr. Scott still has 15 minutes. We'll resume at 5.00 p.m. We'll be sitting -- we'll have Mr. Scott for -- until quarter to 6.00 and then we'll have some time left for re-examination, but I'll ask the registrar to check again. 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honour, if we could go back into private session, please, for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm showing you P 10192 which appears to be a letter by your agency on the 26th of August, 1993, subject "confirmation of consent for transit through the Republic of Croatia." And giving these persons, these listed persons the right to travel through the republic, looking at the first actual paragraph, "... through the Republic of Croatia as a transit country which transit shall last no longer than 48 hours." Apparently on their way to Germany. Is that a document issued by your agency and is it signed by you or someone else?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, the document was not signed by me. Perhaps you can compare it with a document I signed, and you will see there is a difference. On top of that, the document was not issued by the governmental Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees. Judging by the stamp, it was issued by an office in Makarska. There is one other thing I can mention, if it is of any importance. In August 1993, I was on vacation in France at a nun's monastery in Saint-Germain-en-Laye near Paris.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Can you tell us, though, who would have decided then in your absence, for example, in this letter, who decided that 48 hours would be the appropriate time for transit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, I object. It assumes a fact that's not in evidence. He's indicated that this was not issued by his office, so how could he determine, you know, about the 48 hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I didn't -- I don't think he said that. I think the correct answer was he didn't sign it. It says, "Office for Expelled Person, People and Refugees of the Government of the Republic of Croatia," and that's the agency that I understand that he was the head of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He pointed to the stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If it's necessary, Your Honour, I will waste more time by going back through it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I understand it's not your signature, but this is a letter issued by the agency of which you were in charge; correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that this is not my signature. That is number one. Number two, it is correct that it was issued by the regional office of Makarska which was one of the 21 regional offices of the governmental office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As the head of this agency and perhaps you didn't sign this particular document, but given your familiarity with the work of the organisation that you were in charge of, who would decide, then, who in the chain of command, so to speak, would decide that 48 hours was the appropriate time?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning the duration or transit through Croatia, the person issuing such a document could decide on it pursuant to another document, for example, a UNHCR document which guaranteed that the refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina would be moved on to third countries within a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we're going do save some time. 48 hours here is handwritten. The person who signed the document wrote 48 hours. He could have written 72 hours or something else. Mr. Scott wants to know who decides that it's going to be 48 hours. The answer itself is obvious, it's the person who signed and who wrote 48 hours. Did he have the authority to write 48 hours, 72 hours, one week? Did he have that power?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this moment, I cannot know that. I don't know what the legislation there was in place at the time. During that month, I was abroad. In essence, the regional offices did not grant refugee status, only the governmental office was able to do that. Pursuant to the law, they were supposed to ask the central office to grant that. Regional offices were not allowed to grant refugee status, they could only grant displaced person status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can look at the last page of the letter or the bottom of the letter, in any event above the -- your name, I didn't say signature, but above your name, it says, "The above-stated persons in transit cannot request or be given refugee status in the Republic of Croatia." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do see it, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that a standard language that was put on these documents whenever a Muslim was coming from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In respect of whether that person was Muslim or Croatian, if he or she was coming from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and if they only requested transit, they were supposed to be granted such status without granting them refugee status. After having received a transit permit, they could no longer ask for refugee status except in cases in which third countries would not take them and returned them to Croatia. In that case, Croatia was supposed to take them and grant them refugee status.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have a question in regard to the transcript, on line 18, the first words are "In respect of whether" and I wonder whether the witness did not want to say irrespective of whether, I suppose Mr. Karnavas had the same point, I'm sorry if I preempted it. It's actually a question, witness. Did you say something like in respect of or did you say irrespective of?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Dr. Rebic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards. Excuse me, what is it all about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The transcript and it's moving up now, it's on page 14, it's on page 51, line 14 -- line 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Now 18.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to see the text. I said, "Irrespective of whether a person was Muslim or Croat."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I hope this will be clarified once and for all. Yesterday, you've answered questions by the Defence.
