I've asked questions of you too, and the Prosecutor is allowed to put these questions again. I'm going to sum up again. Let's assume we have someone who has a transit visa because he has a guarantee to go to a third country. That person does not have a refugee status; is that right? Fine. Now it's clear for me at least. Mr. Scott. We've spent hours on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. By your leave, I would like to note that the witness's response to your question did not make it in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Witness, can you please repeat your answer to the question I asked you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honour, would you mind repeating the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I said that we spent hours trying to find out whether someone who was in transit, because he or she had a letter of guarantee from a third country, that person would not be granted refugee status by the government of Croatia because he would receive that status, the status of a refugee, in the country where he would be going to. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is my position and that was my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And sir, if I could ask you to look very briefly at the very next document, please, which is 10193. Can you just simply confirm that that is again a similar document in fact issued the same day, the 26th of August, 1993, again giving a person 48 hours to transit through Croatia stating that the person cannot request or receive refugee status in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott, I see the document. The document reflects the same procedure. It is another document issued by the regional office in Makarska. It was not signed by me. It was signed by the head of the regional office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I go on, sir, to just your knowledge of what was happening in connection with these various events when people would show up in Croatia either at the Zagreb mosque or at Gasinci or wherever it was, you told us yesterday I believe that what was happening in Herceg-Bosna really wasn't your remit, and you've told us you were only there on approximately, I don't know, maybe two or three occasions, I think you may have told us now. Is it correct, sir, that in terms of what was happening on the other end of these transactions, so to speak, what was happening at the Ljubuski prison, what was happening at the Heliodrom, what was happening at Dretelj, you had no personal knowledge of that; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, absolutely nothing until we discovered the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, for example, when we talk about these letters of transit or transit visas and letters of guarantee, did you have any knowledge at the time that what was happening would be that people would tell the Muslim prisoners in these camps that if they signed these papers, they could be released from prison. They would have an hour to gather their families and to sign over their property to the HVO and under those conditions they would be able to leave Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. It's argumentative and assumes a lot of facts that are not necessarily established. So -- and the question has been asked and answered and this is argumentative. He can put that in his closing argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm asking whether this witness whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, your objection is dismissed because the same question has been asked of other witnesses. The Trial Chamber is perfectly aware of that possibility and I think it's a good idea to check that with the witness, but I asked the same question myself yesterday. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my question -- you don't know anything about the circumstances which confronted the people who were being released in Bosnia who were getting these letters, who were travelling, who were finding themselves at the Zagreb mosque or finding themselves at Gasinci or some other place. You don't know what drove them to arrive at those locations, do you?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that I had no knowledge, absolutely nothing which can also be seen from my yesterday's answer concerning the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like you to next please go to Exhibit P 10408. Sir, in the interest of time, I'm going to ask for your cooperation, please. This is an article in the Christian Science Monitor dated the 24th of June 1993, and the article indicates that as a result of the conflict between the Croats and Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina that was occurring by the middle of 1993, that in fact the conditions and the treatment that Muslims in refugee centres and Muslims who found themselves in Croatia at the time, the treatment and conditions they confronted were becoming worse. Now, what can you tell us about that in your experience? What complaints, what reports did you receive about the treatment that these Muslims in Croatia were receiving during mid-1993 and thereafter?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I wasn't receiving any such complaints stating that such negative conduct occurred in the Republic of Croatia as we can see is alleged here concerning the Muslims in Croatia. I know that in the press there were many rumours and lots of libel, and I mentioned that in my letter to Mrs. Turkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The short answer is you're telling the Chamber you didn't know anything about any complaints such as these, information such as this?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would like you, please, to go to Exhibit P 00757 in the Prosecution binder. Sir, you told us, I believe, that in the last couple of days that you knew Mr. Mazowiecki, excuse me, my apology, that you had known him, you respected -- if I'm not mistaken, you said you respected him, thought well of him. And this is one of his reports dated the 17th of November, 1992 and if I can please direct your attention to paragraph 62. Fortunately, the paragraphs are numbered so in either translation you should be able to find paragraph 62. And in that paragraph, it says, "In particular, the special rapporteur received information which reveals that ethnic minorities living in the Republic of Croatia remain vulnerable to human rights violations. For example, a number of organisations representing the Serbian minorities assert that the criteria prescribed for obtaining Croatian citizenship discriminate against residents of non-Croatian ethnic origin. The organisation charged that ethnic Croats automatically obtain citizenship regardless of the place or duration of their past residence while minorities living in the Republic of Croatia despite often long-term residents commonly experience up to six month delays or simply refused citizenship." Now, did that situation come to your attention in 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, never was my attention directed at such cases, quite to the contrary, I know that all ethnic minorities received Croatian citizenship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, isn't the problem that in this paragraph, in paragraph 62, we are talking about Serb minorities? As a result, we could understand that Serbian minorities had to wait for a very long time, but as for people coming from Bosnia and Herzegovina because they were considered as Croats because of the Turks and the 16th century or the 12th century, it could be assumed that they would have less difficulties than the Serbs. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't provide a simple answer to a whole host of ambiguous issues here. As regards the difficulties in granting citizenship, there were on the side of Croats as well as on the side of the minorities, I mean Serbs, when I said that, if the paperwork was not orderly. If all the documents requested needed to receive a certificate of citizenship were in order, there were no problems. As far as I understand, there were problems but Croats encountered the same problems if they lacked the necessary documents to be issued with such documents, to be issued with such a certificate. When I referred to ambiguous issues, I had in mind the Muslims in Bosnia who, as of the 16th century, were forced to take on Islam. When I previously spoke about the Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina which declare themselves to be Croatian, I had more recent times in mind, beginning with the late 19th century until the present day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, Witness. This paragraph applies to minorities living, because in English they use the term "living," people living in Croatia. These are not people who come to Croatia and there is a very big difference and it seems that the Special Rapporteur seems to be taking into account that the situation of minorities living in Croatia, i.e., Croatian residents, and not those coming from outside Croatia. Is this the way you understand the text or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My interpretation relates to minorities in the Republic of Croatia. I said that the same problems were experienced by Croats if there were not documents which were in good order, then someone, regardless of whether he was a member of the minority or the majority population had problems because they had to gather all the documents, and this would take months. After all this time today, in Croatia, this is no longer a problem because all the minorities have their status of citizens of Croatia and it's in good order.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we could next please go to Exhibit P 01462 in the Prosecution binder. This is a report, again, by Mr. Mazowiecki dated the 10th of February, 1993. If I can direct your attention, please, to paragraph 118 in which the report expresses concern again, in particular, about the discrimination against minorities who have been refused citizenship and are subjected to verbal and physical abuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point, I will be objecting. I didn't object the first time because I thought maybe the Bench would have objected. Now are we litigating the issues with the Serbs, the Serb minority in Croatia at a time of war when one-third of Croatia was being occupied --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It says minorities. It says minorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, there's a big difference between a minority in a constituent nation and I'm shocked that Mr. Scott doesn't realise the difference and obviously had a problem earlier on, but now we're into a different issue and I am objecting. How large is the scope of the indictment because we haven't been noticed that now we're taking on the Serb minority issue in Croatia during this period and it's up to the Trial Chamber to take control of the situation here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not something I had not noticed. This is the reason why I asked the previous question highlighting the fact that paragraph 62 applies to the Serbs living in Croatia, the Serbian minority in Croatia. So now the Prosecutor continues along this line, but if you want to waste your time this is your problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Where is it in the indictment? Do I have to defend against this? Because that's what I want to know. Am I going to have to defend against this because then we need to call in other witnesses. I'm progressing under the assumption that we have an indictment and the indictment stands as it is and I'm defending against this indictment. Now we're talking about Serbs and a Serb minority at this period. So now we're expanding the indictment and I object on the grounds of jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we're going to solve the problem. Mr. Scott, according to you, do you believe that the Serb minorities are included in the indictment or do you ask this question from a general point of view?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, all the documents that I've shown to the witness in the last few minutes talk about minorities, not just Serbs, and I believe it was Dr. Rebic who told us yesterday that in the Republic of Croatia, there are only about 1 per cent Muslims in the population and that sounds to me like a minority. Whether they come, whether they were born in Croatia, whether they came there from some place else, it is not limited to Serbs, I don't know who suggested it was just talking about Serbs. The paragraphs that I've indicated mention Serbs but it mentions minorities in general. We've spent two days, three days talking about, you know, how all these people were received from Croatia and how they were all treated so well, et cetera so I'm entitled to respond to it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you're not answering the legal problem Mr. Karnavas has raised. For the Prosecution, the Serb minorities against which there was a discrimination, to get the status of Croatians, are they included in the indictment or not? Yes or no? If you say no, you will have -- you then explain that you take the example of Serbian minorities just to show that there was a general discrimination policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What you just said, Your Honour. It's both general and applies to minorities -- I've already answered the question. That there was a general policies and behaviour toward non-Croats, toward non-Croats including both Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I mediate?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We're not going to finish today, Your Honour, if we do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute. I'm waiting for the registrar to tell me first how much time Mr. Scott still has left, then I secondly I would like to remind Mr. Karnavas that if he has additional questions, we -- and wants some redirect, we said that the redirect time would be included in the time allocated to the direct examination of the witness. So theoretically, you have no time for redirect because you've already used all the time you were allocated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... apply this policy. This is the first I've heard. We went through 22 months and the Prosecution never had that policy, now you're imposing a policy on me. I object to that first of all. Second of all, there have been a lot of time being wasted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is in the guidelines. Guideline number 6, it is guideline number 6, read guideline number 6. Mr. Scott, you've used three hours and 43 minutes. So you can now proceed to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in Exhibit P 01462, if I can please ask you to turn to paragraph 136. In the middle of that paragraph, it says, "The entry of refugees into Croatia has been restricted by the government to those holding a letter of a third country guaranteeing their settlement. Croatian Red Cross records show 700.000 registered refugees and displaced persons constituting 17 per cent of the Croatian population. 80 per cent of them live with Croatian families. Most families receive material aid, et cetera, the refugees estimated 540.000 are mostly Muslims from Bosnia and Herzegovina." Excuse me. Well, I -- the question, sir, is did not the situation, the discrimination as to the citizenship apply to the Muslims coming from Bosnia-Herzegovina as we've seen and discussed in the previous document and in this one? "The entry of refugees into Croatia has been restricted by the government to those holding a letter from a third country guaranteeing their settlement." And that's the only way, sir, that people could come in to pass through Croatia at that time. They would into the be given refugee status. And, sir, that's the case I put to you and we've been talking about now for the last two days if we can come right down to it. Sir, from July 1992 forward, undoubtedly a number of Muslims passed through Croatia but it was, it became, and it continued to be the republic of the state of Croatia, these persons would not be given refugee status, they would be allowed, they would be given a transit visa, what was called a transit visa, and allowed to pass through to some other country but not to remain in Croatia, and these repeated documents that we put in front of you show could not apply for and would not receive refugee status. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is absolutely not the case. It's an erroneous conclusion. One cannot draw general conclusions from individual examples. It's true that there was some persons from Bosnia and Herzegovina who asked for transit and they were granted transit only; therefore, they did not have the right to seek refugee status. It's also true that persons who entered the Republic of Croatia, and they did, asking for refugee status were granted refugee status. That's what is true and correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask you, please, to go to Exhibit P 06697. Sir, this is a report from, again, from Mr. Mazowiecki. This one dated the 20th of November, 1993. Directing your attention first of all to paragraph 136. "Since the last report, the situation of the Muslim minority and refugees in Croatia has become an area of concern. According to the 1991 census, 43.469 persons or 0.9 per cent of the population of Croatia identified themselves as Muslims." Now, I'll stop there. I think it was yesterday, perhaps, at some point since you've been testifying you indicated you thought the Muslim population of Croatia was somewhere around 1, perhaps 1 per cent, 1.5 per cent, so would you agree that this is generally consistent with what you've said, that there was something like 1 per cent or less of the Croatian population was Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this report, yes, it's 0.9 per cent, so it corresponds more or less to my report or my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Referring your attention to paragraph 137, do you recall that there was increasing hostility expressed by the Croatian media against the Muslim minority and refugees in Croatia in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to a significant extent. It's understandable that here and there in the Republic of Croatia, there were certain incidents, but I was never informed of any significant incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I direct can your attention, please, to paragraph 139. "There have been reports with many Muslims in Croatia have been denied citizenship although they were either born in Croatia or had lawful residence in Croatia for several years, mentioning several villages." Going on to say, "Almost 200 Muslims are said to have been denied citizenship." Now I'm just citing that as one example. Were you not aware of the continuing concern that the Muslims who found themselves in Croatia during this period were being denied Croatian citizenship?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I'm not aware that someone who had reason to obtain Croatian citizenship and the requisite documents was denied that citizenship. I'm not aware of a single instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In paragraph -- directing your attention to paragraph 143, did you become aware of any situations where Muslims were expelled from Croatia by the Croatian police, handed over to the HVO military police in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you next, please, to go to Exhibit P 07917. Directing your attention, sir, and this is the Mazowiecki report dated the 21st of February, 1994, directing your attention to paragraph 92, directing your attention to the second sentence in that paragraph, "Since the escalation of hostilities between the Bosnian Croat and the government forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there has been a significant increase in harassment of local Muslims and Bosnian Muslim refugees by the authorities, the police, and especially soldiers returning from the front. During his visit to Split, the Special Rapporteur received information concerning illegal and forced evictions," et cetera. Did that information come to your attention during this time?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I was not informed of these matters although there were incidents, but I was not informed, nor was I aware of any significant incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I direct your attention to paragraph 94. Did you ever become aware of continuing concerns, this is the fourth, now, report that we've looked at by Mr. Mazowiecki. In paragraph 94, the continuing concerns with -- discriminatory treatment in connection with citizenship. "The Special Rapporteur has received reports concerning discriminatory treatment of Croatian citizens, in this case, whose place of birth is Bosnia and Herzegovina. They are discriminated against in obtaining employment, social benefits," and did you know that was going on as to people coming from Bosnia-Herzegovina, in particular, during this time? Or did none of this information -- you're saying none of these complaints, none of this information was coming to your attention?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, that's correct. In the ODPR, none of this was drawn to my attention. What it says here about employment, I have to say that in the Republic of Croatia, unfortunately not even citizens of the Republic of Croatia could find work because it was wartime and there were no jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You've said in the course of your -- you've said in the course of your testimony that people were not sent back, they were never sent back to Bosnia-Herzegovina repatriated, returned, against their will. Is that your position, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The ODPR of the Republic of Croatia never returned anyone by force.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You also told us, sir, that indeed there came a time that a policy was adopted when refugee status was revoked or would be revoked when it was determined that according to someone, which is what I'm going to ask you about, decided that it was safe for some people to return to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, you did tell us that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who made the decision as to what location, what locations in Bosnia and Herzegovina were considered "safe" for people to return, refugees to return to?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received information when it came to Herzegovina from the office of -- for displaced persons and other representatives of the local authorities in the municipalities and municipal clubs which were familiar with the local situation. They knew it well. Based on these reports, we knew to which areas persons who had been expelled to go back and they did go back. We acted in the same way in the Republic of Croatia. When some areas were liberated, we learned from the local authorities in the municipalities and then sent the displaced persons from those areas back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Tell me, give me an example, sir. When you say the authorities in the municipalities or municipal club would make a determination that an area was safe. Can you give us a concrete example of that?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are specific examples in the documents. Let's say, for instance, when we revoked refugee status from the area of western Herzegovina, then to that document or attached lists of villages which were safe to which the displaced persons could go back. And we constantly received requests from the Embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina to send refugees back to Bosnia-Herzegovina so that wherever the conditions were in place, Bosnia-Herzegovina could be defended, built up, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, are you telling us that if some social club in Stolac said it was safe for people to come back there, that was good enough for your organisation to start sending people back to Stolac?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite. There were certain conditions that the regional offices and centres for social welfare from the central -- received from the central office. The villages and towns were lists but there were also conditions attached, persons whose houses had been destroyed should not be sent back, persons who were ill, or parents who had children in school, or persons who would not be safe in that place who would be imperilled could not be sent back, and this referred to Muslims in the Croatian areas and vice versa, Croats in the Muslim areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree with me that you could take a given area in Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time and it might very well be -- might be, might be considered safe for one ethnic group but not for another?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did take that into account to avoid putting people in a dangerous situation. That was a very important task of our office in agreement with the UNHCR. When sending displaced persons and refugees back, we took care never to put them in a position where their lives would again be in danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you, for example, at any time concerning the return of refugees or repatriation of refugees to Herzegovina, did you ever exclude or exempt Muslims from that policy on the theory that well, for most -- maybe it was safe for Croats to go back but not for Muslims. Can you tell the Judges whether you ever made that determination?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the regional offices were informed of this. They were informed that what the refugee said about his safety or lack of safety in his place of residence should be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not asking you on an individual case-by-case basis, but can you tell the Judges, did your agency recognise that as to these return policies, that they would apply, for example, as to Herzegovina, they would apply to Croats but not to Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, one it has been asked and answered and two, Herzegovina, it's a fairly large place so -- but it has been asked and answered and on an individual basis, that's the whole point, that you discriminate, you know, where somebody can go and where somebody can't go. The question has been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know where Mr. Karnavas gets this theory about asked and answered. I'm entitled to probe the witness. I don't have to accept the first answer. He -- and he didn't answer my question. He said on "an individual basis" which was not my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So I came back with my original which was: "Was there a determination made in the area of Herzegovina, Herceg-Bosna, any of those areas where your agency decided that, well, look, for these areas, it's safe for Croats to go back, and we're going to apply -- we're going to revoke refugee status of Croats and send them back to Bosnia but for Muslims, we're not because it's not safe for Muslims to go back there." I'm not talking about on an individual case -- I'm talking as two groups of people. That's my question?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer to you is that those areas were, in general, safe for all persons and our office could not know whether all the refugees would be safe on their way back. That is why statements made by individuals were taken into account and respected. If a refugee complained to the main office or the regional office that they personally did not feel safe in the place where they were to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall in a time that -- concerning this issue, excuse me, do you recall that it was only after repeated interventions by either Ms. Turkovic or Mr. Krajisnik that you indicated to your office, to your field offices, that in fact a previous policy that you had directed that you had issued about sending people back, that after their interventions, you changed the policy to make it clear that in Herzegovina, it would not be safe for Muslims to go back? Now, do you not remember that?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I remember a meeting with representatives of the Bosnia-Herzegovina embassy. That meeting has already been mentioned by me in this courtroom. It's correct that I received a letter where difficulties were put forward both by Mrs. Bisera Turkovic and Mr. Jadranko Prlic, and they said that this sort of general return to Bosnia-Herzegovina was not yet possible. We had a long discussion. We made a thorough analysis of the whole issue and together with Bisera, Krijsek [as interpreted], Tadic and Ragus, I immediately sent a clarification to all the regional offices saying that they should adhere to the conditions which were already in place although they had not been expressly listed but the offices should have known about them, so I just reminded the offices that they should send refugees back only in an organised way, gradually, and in agreement with the authorities, the local authorities, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And in addition to this, I stated quite clearly and gave instructions that persons whose homes were destroyed should not be sent back. Persons who were ill and needed medical assistance in Croatia should not be sent back. Persons whose children were in school. And persons who felt threatened in their place of return. All of those were not to be sent back. And that was respected and I had no further complaints either from Mrs. Bisera Turkovic or from Mr. Jadranko Prlic. We harmonised our standpoints in this process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you please tell me how much time is left? Mr. Scott, you have ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to say, just take about 30 seconds on this. We are very concerned, we will let Mr. Karnavas fight his own specific battles about the re-examination of this witness of his, but we are very concerned, Your Honour, because in our submission, Your Honours are misapplying and, with respect, to some extent, misunderstanding your own guideline 6, paragraph 19, and at some point, Your Honour, we would like the opportunity of addressing you on that. We appreciate the time constraints today, but we certainly do not wish any ruling to be made today which might be taken against us when we put down that marker that we do say that what Your Honours have said about the time for direct examination, the time for examination-in-chief also including re-examination time, it is just wrong on your own guidelines. So may we have that opportunity at a convenient point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Scott, you have ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, just a final point on this question and then I'll go on because I thought you had given us a clear answer, but I'm not sure as your answer continued it was. I put it to you, sir, that in October of 1993, after repeated interventions by Muslim authorities, that you clarified very specifically that the direction to return to repatriate refugees to Herzegovina only -- would only apply to Croat refugees and not to Muslims. Now, do you remember that? Can you confirm that for us or not?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that but I can confirm in principle, in general, that in Herzegovina it was quite safe for Croats to return and that Croat refugees were able to return and no longer needed to enjoy refugee status. As regards Muslims, since the Serbs in the former JNA had occupied their areas and at that time, this amounted to about 70 per cent of Bosnia, return was not safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir are, I'm going to -- we'll take it at that because we have to finish up here in the next few minutes. Let us go back to the situation regarding the Dretelj camp because you went to that camp with Dr. Granic and Mr. Prlic and others in late September 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct that I was there but I visited only once. The way it was interpreted to me, it could mean that I visited more than once but it was actually only on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Around the 23rd or 24th of September 1993, sir, you went to visit the Dretelj camp and then there was a press conference, I believe, later at Medjurgorje. You recall that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when you went to the Dretelj camp and you visited that camp at the time, can you recall to the Judges the condition of the prisoners, the men who were being held in that camp, what was their condition as you observed it?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as the government of the Republic of Croatia --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, when you were at the camp, what did you see, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll answer. First I have to have a dependent clause and then I will give you my independent clause. That's the rule of the Croatian language, Croatian syntax. As soon as the Croatian government learned what was happening, I went with Professor Granic, I was tasked by the government to go there to see what the situation was and to resolve it on the spot; that is, to take over the prisoners there and to give them refugee status in the Republic of Croatia and accommodate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, what was the condition of the men that you saw there when you were there in September 1993? That's my question, sir. And you know my time is limited.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very hard, after more than 15 years, to remember what these people looked like. I did not have the impression that they looked the way some media describe it, but to be a prisoner is certainly not pleasant and cannot have good consequences for a person, but only bad ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, on every account, I dare say, every account and the witnesses that have come before this Chamber, some of whom were prisoners, have made it very clear that the condition of these men was absolutely horrendous, they were emaciated, they were sick. You're saying you didn't see that or didn't seem to you a big deal or what are you telling these Judges?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Scott, that's not what I said. I said I don't remember precisely what they looked like, but they were certainly in a miserable condition because every prisoner by virtue of being a prisoner is in a miserable condition. I didn't have time to inspect individuals. Our stay in Dretelj was very brief and my task was to get these people out as soon as possible, as urgently as possible and accommodate them as refugees in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The answer you gave a moment ago on page 72 line 23, 24 was: "I did not have the impression they looked the way some media described it ..." and frankly that came across as, they didn't look that bad to me. Now, are you changing your answer? Did you see these men or not or maybe you didn't even go there. Please tell the Judges.

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will say that some media stated that they were all like skeletons. I didn't see any skeletons. That's what I meant to say. I didn't mean to say that they were in good condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May I ask you, please, to turn to Exhibit P 10423. P 10423. I may need the usher's assistance if he doesn't find it right away because of the time. Sir, in the diary that you provided which was marked as an exhibit on Monday, you -- for an entry in that document for the -- at 10.00 on the 26th of April, 1993, you made this entry: "Darinko Tadic, head of office for refugees and displaced persons in Mostar. A conversation about the problems that Mr. Darinko Tadic faces not to let the BiH citizens to the HVO territory unless they were born there, all others are to be sent to Tuzla, Zenica, or abroad; provide assistance in issuing customs permits for the aid that is destined also for Herzegovina." What can you tell us about that conversation, sir, with Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first part of this entry refers to Tadic's statement that the Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees in Herceg-Bosna was not allowing citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina who had not been born in Herzegovina to come to Herzegovina but that those who were not born in Herzegovina were being sent by them to Tuzla, Zenica, or elsewhere and that they were only allowing those who were born in Herzegovina to go there. He asked me in the case of persons going to Croatia to provide assistance and also to ensure assistance with the customs, and they could only do that through me to make sure that the customs assisted when aid was coming from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, wait a minute. What did you have to do with customs? You were ODPR. What did you have to do with controlling customs and what went in and out of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ADALBERT REBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, well that's what I said in my previous response. I didn't have anything to do with customs. All I could do was mediate, ask the customs authorities for assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Rebic. I want to thank you for coming to The Hague and giving your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. As indicated by the Trial Chamber, there will be no redirect for -- and there is no redirect for the party calling the witness unless that time is taken from the examination-in-chief and we believe that there should be no redirect by the other Defence counsel either, but following Mr. Stewart's intervention, we'll consider the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For the record, I do wish to state for the record you are violating my client's rights, his human rights, you are violating, we have time and I just want to make sure that we're absolutely clear that this time it is not due to some exit strategy by the UN but rather this is a calculated attempt by the Trial Chamber to deny Dr. Prlic's human rights. I just want to make sure that the record is very clear. You made your ruling, I respect your ruling. I made my record for the appeal and for the public to see how we are being treated in this courtroom. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, let me answer. Mr. Karnavas, we issued a ruling that was extremely clear. We stated that time dedicated to re-examination should be deducted from the time granted for examination in chief. In other words, if you request four hours for a witness, you should use three and a half hours for the examination in chief and half an hour for redirect. That's your problem it's not the Chamber's problem. That's the meaning of guideline number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I requested five hours. I requested five hours. You said four. I got some additional time. That's number one. Number two, there's time on the clock. Number three, you gave me a certain amount of hours to put on my case. I'd asked for 146 hours or 150, I got 90, 95, whatever. I'm entitled to use that time how I see fit. As long as I'm doing my job. As long as I can demonstrate that what I'm asking are relevant questions and questions that are not repetitive, I should be entitled to put on case. You've made your case, I understand it, I respect your decision, I'm on the record. This is a violation of my client's human rights. Very well. We can go now and dismiss for the rest of the week. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. I actually might have something to say with Your Honour's permission. Your Honour said you would consider it. I assume that I'm now able to make submissions on the point which I raised a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That should be enough, Your Honour, thank you. It's -- Your Honour just said a few moments ago that you've made an extremely clear ruling or given an extremely clear guideline. Your Honour, may we look at your guideline 6 paragraph 19 and see what it actually says. It says that -- well, 18 is worth looking at, at that point, when this order was made on the 24th of April, the Trial Chamber said in paragraph 18 under guideline 6 that it would render a separate decision regarding the time that the Defence teams would have for presentation of their cases, which you did very shortly afterwards, you gave certification in that decision and that is under appeal. So the question of the overall time for the Defence cases is certainly very contentious and is under appeal now. Paragraph 19 of your guideline says that the time allocated to a Defence team to present its case shall first include the time used for the direct examination and re-examination of its Defence witnesses. Now, Your Honour, we don't like that. I want to make it clear that the Defence do not like that guideline, and we are appealing the whole matter as I've indicated, but what it clearly means as it stands is that you add together -- if we've got 55 hours for the Petkovic case, that you add together time taken for examination-in-chief or direct examination with time taken in re-examination, and all that time together is to be done within the 55 hours. And going right back to the very beginning of these time allocations, when you ordered 400 hours for the Prosecution case, that was how it was done. It was to be the direct examination, examination-in-chief, and re-examination were all to be done within that 400 hours. And we know the painful history of all the reductions and so on but that was the basic position. That's quite different from what Your Honours are now saying which is when a specific allocation is given for a specific witness of time for direct examination, that if that's all used up, then there is no time left for re-examination. Mr. Karnavas is 100 per cent right. That is not the way the matter was dealt with when the Prosecution examined its witnesses. If it was given three hours for examination in chief, it had -- usually you could say, use the three hours for examination in chief, there was never any suggestion that they wouldn't also be able to re-examine that witness; although, according to the Chamber's guidelines on the -- if you like the bigger issue, the macro issue as opposed to the micro issue of witnesses, that time was to be counted to the overall allocation. Your Honour, I just add this, the incorrect, as we strongly submit, the incorrect interpretation of Your Honour's own guideline is completely unworkable. You're given 4 hours to examine in chief. You've got a choice between not using the whole of that four hours in case, as a result of the cross-examination, you might need time for re-examination. You can't possibly know until you've heard the cross-examination. Well, sorry, if there is a cross-examination as my learned friends remind me, but you can't know until you've heard the cross-examination how much you're going to need for re-examination. Nobody can say that. So you either give up some of your time in case there is a cross-examination in case you need to re-examine, or you end up with the result that Your Honours' indication earlier on this evening would lead to which we say, frankly, is a ridiculous result, we put it as strongly as that, as you now say Mr. Karnavas has done, used up all his time and doesn't get to re-examination when elementary justice requires that once there's been a cross-examination, if there is a legitimate basis and if there are legitimate questions to be asked in re-examination, it simply cannot be right and it cannot be a fair trial to prevent a party from doing it. Irrelevant questions, Your Honours can always stop those if there isn't a genuine re-examination, but we do submit that what Your Honour indicated about 10 or 15 minutes ago is completely wrong and certainly it means, although there is not much time left today, it certainly means, but he can fight his own battles as I've said, if Mr. Karnavas genuinely needs to re-examine then the Petkovic Defence position in support of him would be that and he should have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one word on this point concerning the status of refugees. We have spent about almost two weeks because we had two witnesses who discussed this issue. Okay. So we could spend three weeks and months if you want, but I believe that I have sufficient information about the issue. If I thought that we would have needed additional questions, re-examinations in this field, I would have allocated additional time. On the other hand, I have asked a lot of questions on this issue. Paragraph 19 of guideline number 6 is clear enough on this point. It clearly indicates that the party examining must take into account the fact that re-examinations are included in the time allocated and if you all believe that this witness is important, nothing impedes you from asking him to come back. This is what I wanted to say. So witness, I would like to thank you for coming here and I would like to wish you a nice trip back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, I really do not wish to fight Mr. Karnavas's battles but some of his battles are also our battles, and if it's not using too Karnavasian language, Your Honour, the Petkovic Defence will not accept a position where Your Honours take it upon yourselves to decide for us whether we need to re-examine. Once we start re-examining, if we go into completely irrelevant, completely useless areas, then Your Honours of course have the overriding right to stop that because that's abusive and it's unprofessional, but I'm quite confident that Ms. Alaburic is not going to do that and I hope I don't do it myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart, redirects are authorised based on the decision of the Trial Chamber. This is in the rules and that you know as well as I do. It is mentioned in the rules, re-examinations authorised about the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: With respect, may I ask a question it's not usual. I don't understand which rule Your Honour is referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart, if you have any problems, do it in writing and we will answer your questions. Say it in writing and we will answer. That's what I want to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, I'm not going to be so insolent as to invite Your Honours to answer my question in writing, but I do need an answer to the question because I simply do not understand now what point Your Honour is making, what rule Your Honour is referring to, and we cannot make sensible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart. First of all, the additional time for the questions of the party examining is included in the time decided -- allocated by the Chamber before the direct examination and second point, there are no redirect for the other teams, Defence teams. Now, if you do not agree, you can appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... re-examination of Mr. Karnavas's witness. I'm putting down a marker for the Petkovic team that when it comes to our witnesses, it is not for the Trial Chamber to decide at the end of cross-examination that we have no re-examination. It is for us in the first place to decide whether we need probably to re-examine subject to the overriding ways of the Trial Chamber to rule it out as irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the reason why I'm telling you that you should state it in writing and we will answer. I now would like to thank the witness and I would like to ask the usher to take him out, to accompany him, and next week we will have another witness, a witness of Mr. Prlic, he will be here for four days as mentioned in the filings. That's all I meant to say. Well, I wish you a nice trip back, Witness, because you told us that this week you had to travel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I thank you for your good wishes and I wish you all success in your work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
